etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English abbreviaten, from Latin abbreviātus, perfect passive participle of abbreviō (“to shorten”), formed from ad + breviō (“shorten”), from brevis (“short”). Alternatively, a back-formation from abbreviation. Doublet of abridge.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To shorten by omitting parts or details. [Attested from around (1350 to 1470) until the late 17th century.][2]

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Dispatch. XXV.”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC, pages 142–143:
quote.text: But it is one Thing, to Abbreuiate by Contracting, Another by Cutting off:  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To speak or write in a brief manner. [Attested from the late 16th century until the early 17th century.][2]
(transitive) To make shorter; to shorten (in time); to abridge; to shorten by ending sooner than planned. [First attested from around (1350 to 1470).][2]

quote.citation: 2019 November 21, Samanth Subramanian, “How our home delivery habit reshaped the world”, in Katharine Viner, editor, The Guardian‎[1], London: Guardian News & Media, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2019-11-21:
quote.text: But as delivery schedules have dwindled into hours, even the gigantic warehouse full of stuff in a central place such as the triangle is proving insufficient. Now, companies also need smaller distribution centres around the country, to respond rapidly to orders and to abbreviate the last mile as much as possible.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To reduce a word or phrase by means of contraction or omission to a shorter recognizable form. [First attested in the late 16th century.][2]
(transitive, mathematics) To reduce to lower terms, as a fraction.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Late Latin abbreviātus, perfect passive participle of abbreviō (“abbreviate”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Abbreviated; abridged; shortened. [Attested from around (1350 to 1470) until the late 17th century][2]

quote.citation: 1871, John Earle, The Philology of the English Tongue:
quote.text: The curt form of gent as a less ceremonious substitute for the full expression of ‘gentleman,’ had once made considerable way, but its career was blighted in a court of justice. It is about twenty years ago that two young men, being brought before a London magistrate, described themselves as ‘gents.’ The magistrate said that he considered that a designation little better than ‘blackguard.’ The abbreviate form has never been able to recover that shock.

definitions.definition: (biology) Having one part relatively shorter than another or than the ordinary type. [First attested in the mid 19th century.][2]
